South Korea wants to pay up to seventy-five thousand dollars for a single tip. Not about a robbery. About cheating on one exam.
And if you're caught, you could be banned from that exam for ten years.
Today, more than half a million people sat that exam. So, three questions. What is this exam? Why is Korea this worried? And how much of this is actually in place yet?
First, the exam. The Suneung is Korea's College Scholastic Ability Test, the national college entrance exam.
This year, five hundred fifty-one thousand, eight hundred sixty-four people applied.
It ran today at one thousand three hundred twelve test centers, from eight forty in the morning to five forty-five in the evening.
And the whole country moves around it.
The stock market opened and closed an hour later, to ease morning traffic. Seoul added twenty-seven subway runs.
From one oh five to one forty in the afternoon, during the English listening section, every takeoff and landing in the country was suspended.
Planes already in the air had to stay above three kilometers.
Even the sky has to be quiet.
And people abroad watch it every year. Last year, the English questions went viral, as native English speakers shared their attempts to answer them.
Why go this far? The Korea Herald puts it simply. In Korea, the university you attend can heavily influence your career.
The Associated Press goes further. Jobs, social standing, and even marriage prospects can depend on it.
So why the bounty? Because of a different exam.
Last weekend, the top scorer on Korea's certified tax accountant exam confessed that he cheated with the help of AI and digital devices.
He used a hidden camera and generative AI during the exam. He has been questioned by police as a suspect, and he apologized to the other test-takers.
According to Korean media, he got one hundred fifty-nine of one hundred sixty questions right in the first round.
And the investigation could expand to other national exams.
And it wasn't the first warning.
In June, Korea reported its first cheating cases using AI smart glasses, on the TOEIC English test.
In October, smart glasses were also caught on some university essay exams.
Glasses used to just help you see the test.
So one question hung over this week. Could it happen on the Suneung?
The government's answer: check everything.
The prime minister said proctors would inspect every test-taker's glasses and watches, and even collars, sleeves and buttons.
Every one of the one thousand three hundred twelve test centers had staff assigned just to spot smart glasses. In Seoul, they were trained to look for thick frames and features around the lenses.
Test-takers were handed stickers to cover the buttons on their clothes, to block miniature cameras.
Bags stayed outside the exam rooms, and officials would check whether any devices inside them were switched on.
All electronic devices were banned from exam rooms. Test-takers could bring in only pencils.
Not handing in a device counts as cheating, even if it's never used. And test-takers who acted suspiciously could be checked with metal detectors.
The prime minister also asked the science ministry to look into turning off public Wi-Fi at test sites during the exam.
And then, the phones. Two emergency alerts were set to reach nearly every phone in the country, loud even on silent, to catch any phone that had not been handed in.
About seventy-five thousand proctors were on duty, plus around eight thousand four hundred extra staff.
Blip would have to leave his whole face in the hallway.
Now, the money.
On Tuesday, President Lee Jae Myung called exam cheating a grave crime that undermines social trust.
In a post on X, he said the government plans to offer over one hundred million won per confirmed case, to people who report cheating with advanced gadgets.
And he added a message for anyone thinking about it: do not ruin your life by needlessly gambling on a stroke of luck. Give it up, both for yourself and everyone else.
A day later, the prime minister's office put it differently: up to one hundred million won, if the tip is confirmed as cheating. That's about seventy-five thousand dollars.
Over, then up to. Two small words, a big difference.
Then the penalties. A ten-year ban from the exam. Criminal charges, with up to five years in prison. And college students who cheat would be expelled from their schools.
People who knowingly sell devices made for cheating, and the people who buy them, would be investigated too.
But here's the catch. Much of this is not in place yet.
The reward needs new rules. The government says it will write them quickly, and is pushing to apply them from this exam.
The ten-year ban needs a law. The ruling Democratic Party says it is drafting a special law to extend the ban from one year to ten, and wants to fast-track it so it applies to this week's exam.
Whether that can happen in time is still an open question.
From November twentieth, a task force led by the prime minister will work with global AI companies and telecom firms to look for cheating cases.
And the prime minister has said companies that run AI chatbots agreed to help with investigations after the exam.
Not everyone thinks this is the right fix.

A senior official at a teachers' union told the Korea Herald: collecting electronic devices and leaving them outside is something we have already been doing. I don't think this is really an effective response.
The union's bigger complaint: instead of new systems, the plan mostly gives teachers more duties.
The education minister has said the ministry is considering more detection equipment for future exams, including radio-frequency detectors and metal detectors.
And abroad, people noticed. One Reddit user, quoted by the Korea Times, wrote: suddenly, everyone is a proctor now. False accusation drama is going to be wild.
The vice education minister's answer, earlier this week: we believe we are in a situation where excessive measures are necessary.
So, how much of this is real? The checks happened today. The bounty and the ten-year ban are still being written.
And the bigger question is still there. If AI can answer the test, what should the test be testing? Tell Blip in the comments.
